# Overview

Zentangler is an MAE-first R package for generic multiview parallel mediation
analysis. The package is designed for studies where an exposure variable `X` may
influence many candidate mediators distributed across multiple omics or assay
views, and those mediators may in turn be associated with an outcome `Y`.

The active method focuses on the parallel multiview mediation setting:

```text
X -> mediator in view 1 -> Y
X -> mediator in view 2 -> Y
...
X -> mediator in view K -> Y
```

The package is intentionally generic. A view can be microbiome, metabolome,
proteome, transcriptome, pathway abundance, clinical biomarkers, imaging-derived
features, or any other numeric feature matrix. Zentangler does not assume exactly
two views.

The public user-facing input is a `MultiAssayExperiment` object. This is useful
for Bioconductor package development because it keeps assay data, sample mapping,
and phenotype variables in one coordinated container.

The main entry point is `zentangler()`:

```text
zentangler(mae, model = c("parallel", "sequential"), x_var, y_var, route = NULL, ...)
```

`model = "parallel"` (the default, and the focus of this vignette) treats every
feature of every view as a candidate mediator. `model = "sequential"` chains
mediators along an ordered route of views, `X -> M1 -> ... -> Mk -> Y` (see the
short example near the end, and the sequential vignette). All further
arguments are passed to `fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler()` or
`fit_sequential_zentangler()`, which can also be called directly; their help
pages document every option.

# Statistical target

For each mediator feature `j` in view `k`, Zentangler estimates two main pieces
of evidence.

The first piece is the A-path:

```text
Does X associate with mediator j in view k?
```

This gives an A-path coefficient `a_hat` (column `a`) and A-path p-value `p_a`.

The second piece is the B-path:

```text
After accounting for X and other selected mediators, does mediator j associate
with Y?
```

This gives a B-path coefficient `b` and B-path p-value `p_b`.

The main mediation score is:

```text
score_j = a_hat_j * b_j
```

A positive score means the A-path and B-path have the same sign. A negative score
means the A-path and B-path have opposite signs. Larger absolute scores are used
as a ranking measure.

Important scientific distinction: `score = a*b` remains the mediator-level
screening and ranking score. Zentangler separately reports causal direct,
indirect, and total effect summaries using a parametric g-computation layer
fitted on the significant mediators (`q_primary <= effect_q_threshold`). These
causal summaries are conditional on the selected mediator set and on the usual mediation identification assumptions; they are not
a replacement for sensitivity analysis or a final selective-inference proof.

# Input data contract

The primary input is a `MultiAssayExperiment`.

Zentangler expects:

1. One or more experiments in `experiments(mae)`.
2. Each experiment represents one view.
3. Features are numeric.
4. Samples can be aligned to `colData(mae)`.
5. `colData(mae)` contains either a numeric exposure variable `x_var`, or the
   case/time columns needed by `study_design`.
6. `colData(mae)` contains the outcome variable `y_var`.
7. Optional covariates are also stored in `colData(mae)`.

Most Bioconductor assays are stored as features x samples. Zentangler extracts
these into sample x feature matrices internally. Plain matrix-like experiments
are also supported when sample IDs can be mapped.

# Creating a small MAE

The example below simulates a small `MultiAssayExperiment` with a known
mediation structure, so that we can later check which mediators Zentangler
recovers. In real analyses, you would replace these simulated matrices with
your own assay data.

The simulator draws a binary exposure `X` and an `age` covariate, three views
with 120, 80 and 50 features, and a few true mediators per view with an A-path
(`X -> M`) and a B-path (`M -> Y`). It stores a continuous outcome `Y`, a binary
outcome `Y_binary`, and a survival outcome (`time`, 0/1 `status`), together
with a few design columns used later in this vignette. The true mediators are
returned as `"view::feature"` ids.

```{r}
library(Zentangler)
library(MultiAssayExperiment)
library(SummarizedExperiment)

simulate_mediation_mae <- function(n = 200,
                                   p = c(view1 = 120, view2 = 80, view3 = 50),
                                   n_true = c(view1 = 2, view2 = 2, view3 = 1),
                                   a_effect = 0.6,
                                   b_effect = 0.5,
                                   direct_effect = 0.4,
                                   seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  sample_ids <- sprintf("sample_%03d", seq_len(n))
  X <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
  age <- rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10)
  age_c <- (age - 50) / 10

  lin <- direct_effect * X + 0.2 * age_c
  truth <- character(0)
  experiments <- list()
  for (v in names(p)) {
    M <- matrix(rnorm(n * p[[v]]), nrow = n)
    colnames(M) <- sprintf("%s_f%03d", v, seq_len(p[[v]]))
    k <- seq_len(n_true[[v]])
    M[, k] <- M[, k] + a_effect * X + 0.2 * age_c       # A-path
    lin <- lin + b_effect * rowSums(M[, k, drop = FALSE]) # B-path
    truth <- c(truth, paste(v, colnames(M)[k], sep = "::"))
    rownames(M) <- sample_ids
    # SummarizedExperiment stores assays as features x samples.
    experiments[[v]] <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(abundance = t(M)))
  }

  event_time <- rexp(n, rate = 0.1 * exp(0.5 * (lin - mean(lin))))
  censor_time <- rexp(n, rate = 0.05)
  pheno <- DataFrame(
    X = X,
    age = age,
    Y = lin + rnorm(n),
    Y_binary = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lin - mean(lin))),
    time = pmin(event_time, censor_time),
    status = as.integer(event_time <= censor_time),
    group = ifelse(X == 1, "case", "control"),
    visit = sample(c("T0", "T1"), n, replace = TRUE),
    subject_id = rep(sprintf("subject_%03d", seq_len(ceiling(n / 2))), each = 2)[seq_len(n)],
    row.names = sample_ids
  )

  list(
    mae = MultiAssayExperiment(experiments = ExperimentList(experiments), colData = pheno),
    truth = truth
  )
}

sim <- simulate_mediation_mae()
mae <- sim$mae
truth <- sim$truth
mae
truth
```

# Running the main model

A minimal fit only needs the exposure and the outcome. All other options have
defaults: SIS screening per view, a multiview cooperative-learning outcome model
(`fusion = "multiview"`, whose agreement parameter `rho` runs from 0, early
fusion, to 1, late fusion, and is chosen by cross-validation), a de-biased
B-path (`b_inference = "debiased"`), and composite-null FDR control
(`fdr_joint = "hdmt"`).

```{r}
fit <- zentangler(
  mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  covariates = "age",
  sis_n = 25,
  fdr_method = "BH",
  fdr_scope = "global"
)

fit
summary(fit)
```

`zentangler(mae, ...)` with the default `model = "parallel"` is the same fit
as `fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(mae, ...)`; the remaining examples call
the latter directly where its options are discussed.

## Transforming count and compositional views

Microbiome counts, relative abundances and other non-negative, skewed views are
usually transformed before modeling. The `transform` argument sets the
transformation per view:

- `"none"` (default): use the values as they are.
- `"log"`: `log(x + pseudocount)`.
- `"clr"`: centered log-ratio, `log(x + pseudocount)` minus the per-sample mean
  of the logged values over the view's features. CLR removes the
  sequencing-depth (closure) effect, so it suits compositional data such as
  taxon counts or relative abundances.

A single value applies to every view; a vector named by view sets each view
separately, and unnamed views stay untransformed. `pseudocount` (one value or
named by view) is added before taking logs; by default it is half the smallest
positive value in each view. Both transforms need non-negative data.

To illustrate, we replace `view1` by a small count view `taxa` (30 taxa with
varying sequencing depth) whose first two taxa carry the signal of the true
mediators `view1_f001` and `view1_f002`:

```{r}
set.seed(2)
m <- t(assay(mae[["view1"]])[c("view1_f001", "view1_f002"), ])
depth <- rpois(nrow(m), 5000)
log_rate <- matrix(rnorm(30), nrow = nrow(m), ncol = 30, byrow = TRUE)
log_rate[, 1:2] <- log_rate[, 1:2] + 0.8 * m
props <- exp(log_rate) / rowSums(exp(log_rate))
taxa <- matrix(rpois(length(props), depth * props), nrow = nrow(m))
dimnames(taxa) <- list(rownames(m), sprintf("taxon_%02d", 1:30))

mae_counts <- MultiAssayExperiment(
  experiments = c(
    experiments(mae)[c("view2", "view3")],
    ExperimentList(taxa = SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = t(taxa))))
  ),
  colData = colData(mae)
)

fit_clr <- zentangler(
  mae_counts,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  covariates = "age",
  transform = c(taxa = "clr"),
  sis_n = 25
)
fit_clr$settings$mae_view_map
zentangler_mediators(fit_clr, q_threshold = 0.25)[
  , c("omics", "mediator", "a", "b", "score", "q_primary")
]
```

With the CLR transform, `taxon_01` and `taxon_02` are found alongside the true
`view2` and `view3` mediators. In real data, transforms can be mixed across
views, for example `transform = c(species = "clr", metabolites = "log")`, and
the pseudocount set explicitly with `pseudocount = c(species = 0.5)`.

# Study Design Helpers

The default `study_design = "standard"` uses `x_var` directly. This remains the
right interface when the exposure is already numeric.

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y"
)
```

For case-control data, Zentangler can create the 0/1 exposure internally:

```{r}
fit_case <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  y_var = "Y",
  study_design = "case_control",
  case_var = "group",
  control_level = "control",
  case_level = "case"
)
```

For a time-only analysis, choose one reference and one comparison time point:

```{r}
fit_time <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  y_var = "Y",
  study_design = "time",
  time_var = "visit",
  time_ref = "T0",
  time_compare = "T1"
)
```

For data with both case/control status and time points, use
`study_design = "case_control_time"`. The `exposure_role` controls whether the
exposure is the time contrast, the case-control contrast, or the case-by-time
interaction. With `add_design_covariates = TRUE`, Zentangler adjusts for the
remaining design terms.

```{r}
fit_case_time <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  y_var = "Y",
  study_design = "case_control_time",
  case_var = "group",
  control_level = "control",
  case_level = "case",
  time_var = "visit",
  time_ref = "T0",
  time_compare = "T1",
  exposure_role = "interaction"
)
```

# Stage 1: A-path estimation

The A-stage asks whether each candidate mediator is associated with the exposure.
This is done separately within each view.

For mediator `j` in view `k`, the basic model is:

```text
M_jk = alpha_jk + a_jk * X + covariate terms + error_jk
```

The coefficient `a_jk` is the A-path estimate, stored in column `a`. The
p-value testing whether `a_jk = 0` is stored as `p_a`. Covariates are adjusted
for in every model (A-path, outcome model and causal-effect models).

Zentangler provides three A-stage options, chosen per view with `a_stage_model`.

## HIMA-like linear A-stage

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  a_stage_model = "lm",
  sis_n = 25
)
```

This option uses transparent univariate linear modeling. It is simple, fast, and
close in spirit to the first screening step used in HIMA-style pipelines.

## MaAsLin2 A-stage

```{r}
if (requireNamespace("Maaslin2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit_maaslin2 <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
    mae = mae,
    x_var = "X",
    y_var = "Y",
    a_stage_model = "maaslin2",
    maaslin2_args = list(
      random_effects = "subject_id",
      normalization = "NONE",
      transform = "NONE",
      analysis_method = "LM",
      output = file.path(tempdir(), "maaslin2_a_stage")
    ),
    sis_n = 25
  )
}
```

This option is useful when the A-stage needs MaAsLin2-style modeling, especially
when repeated measures or subject-level random effects are important. In this
mode, covariates and random effects are modeled directly by MaAsLin2 rather than
by the internal linear model. `maaslin2_args` is passed straight to
`Maaslin2::Maaslin2()`, so its names are MaAsLin2's own arguments:
`random_effects`, `normalization`, `transform`, `analysis_method`,
`standardize`, `reference`, `min_prevalence`, `output` and so on. Zentangler
supplies the data, adds the exposure and covariates to `fixed_effects`, and
defaults to no normalization or transformation, LM, and no prevalence or
abundance filtering. MaAsLin2's own `transform` is separate from Zentangler's
`transform` argument; use one or the other, not both.

## Tweedieverse A-stage

This chunk is not run; it shows the call for an MAE with a `species` count
view.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
if (requireNamespace("Tweedieverse", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit_tweedie <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
    mae = microbiome_mae,
    x_var = "X",
    y_var = "Y",
    transform = c(species = "clr"),
    a_stage_model = c(species = "tweedieverse", metabolites = "lm"),
    tweedieverse_args = list(random_effects = "SubjectID"),
    sis_n = 25
  )
}
```

`"tweedieverse"` fits per-feature Tweedie GLMs (`Tweedieverse::Tweedieverse()`)
to the untransformed values of a view: counts, relative abundances or
continuous data such as metabolite intensities, with or without excess zeros.
It models zeros, skewness and overdispersion without a pseudocount; data with
negative values are fitted with the Gaussian case (`p = 0`).
The view's `transform` (here CLR) is still used by the outcome model and the
causal effects; Tweedieverse only supplies screening and `p_a`, and for
non-negative data its `a` is a log fold change per unit of `X`. `tweedieverse_args` is passed straight to
`Tweedieverse()` (one list, or a list per view). Install it with
`remotes::install_github("himelmallick/Tweedieverse")`. In small samples its
p-values can be somewhat anti-conservative, so prefer
`fdr_scope = "within_view"` or `"lm"` there.

# Stage 2: Screening

High-dimensional mediation can involve hundreds or thousands of mediators per
view. Zentangler therefore supports screening before fitting the Y model.

The default screening strategy is SIS-style filtering:

```text
Keep the top N mediators per view.
```

The ranking can be based on either the magnitude of the A-path estimate or the
A-path p-value.

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  screen_method = "sis",
  sis_n = 50,
  sis_rank = "abs_a"
)
```

To turn this off and pass all filtered numeric mediators into the B-stage:

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  screen_method = "none"
)
```

Turning off screening can increase power when sample size is large enough, but it
also makes the Y-stage larger and can be less stable in small sample settings.
At most `debias_max_targets` (default 200) mediators are de-biased in the
B-stage; with many unscreened features, increase it or the remaining mediators
are treated as untested (a warning is issued).

# Stage 3: Multiview B-stage fusion

After A-stage estimation and optional screening, Zentangler fits a Y-stage model
that includes `X`, selected mediators from the views, and optional covariates.

The conceptual model is:

```text
Y = direct X term + selected mediator terms + covariate terms + error
```

The mediator coefficient from this stage is the B-path estimate `b`.

The outcome model is chosen with `fusion`:

- `fusion = "multiview"` (default): multiview cooperative learning.
- `fusion = "integrated_learner"`: supplementary IntegratedLearner-style
  fusion, with `integrated_learner_fusion = "late"` (default) or `"early"`.

## Multiview cooperative learning (main engine)

```{r}
fit <- zentangler(
  mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y"
)
fit$settings$rho_used # agreement parameter chosen by cross-validation
fit$settings$rho_cv   # CV error for each candidate rho
```

This is the default and main engine. It fits the outcome model with cooperative
learning from the `multiview` package: each view gets its own sparse
coefficients, and an agreement penalty `rho` encourages the views' fitted
contributions to agree. `rho` lies in \[0, 1\]: `rho = 0` is early fusion (one
model on the concatenated views) and `rho = 1` is late fusion, with values in
between interpolating. `rho` and `lambda` are tuned jointly by
cross-validation over `rho_grid` (default `c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1)`), so
the data choose the degree of fusion. Supply `rho` to fix the value instead:

```{r}
fit_rho <- zentangler(
  mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  rho = 0.5
)
summary(fit_rho)$model[, c("fusion", "rho")]
```

Gaussian, binomial and survival outcomes are supported. With `multiview` 1.0,
Cox fits with `rho > 0` often do not converge; such `rho` values are dropped
from the grid with a warning, so survival fits may end up at `rho = 0`.

The IntegratedLearner-style early and late fusion below are supplementary
alternatives, useful as sensitivity analyses or when `multiview` is not
installed.

## IntegratedLearner-style early fusion

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  glmnet_alpha = 1,
  lambda_choice = "lambda.1se"
)
```

Early fusion concatenates all selected mediators from all views into one design
matrix and fits one penalized model. This lets all views compete directly inside
a single model. It is simple and often a good first option.

`glmnet_alpha = 1` gives lasso. Values between 0 and 1 give elastic net. For
example:

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  glmnet_alpha = 0.5
)
```

## IntegratedLearner-style late fusion

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "late",
  glmnet_alpha = 1
)
```

Late fusion fits view-specific penalized models first and then combines the
view-level fitted signals in a meta model. This can help preserve view-level
structure and can be useful when views have very different feature scales or
feature counts.

## Survival outcomes

For time-to-event outcomes, use Cox survival models by setting
`y_family = "survival"` and providing follow-up time and event columns.

```{r}
fit_surv <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_family = "survival",
  survival_time_var = "time",
  survival_event_var = "status",
  covariates = "age",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  b_inference = "debiased"
)
```

Survival outcomes support both outcome models; with the default multiview model
`rho > 0` values that do not converge are dropped (see above), so the example
uses the supplementary early fusion directly. The B-stage can use
`b_inference = "debiased"` (de-sparsified Cox lasso) or
`b_inference = "bootstrap"`.

# Stage 4: B-path inference

The default B-stage inference is a de-biased (de-sparsified) lasso on the joint
outcome model `Y ~ X + C + all screened mediators`. Every screened mediator is a
target, so `b`, `se_b` and `p_b` exist for the whole screened set. Gaussian and
binary outcomes use nodewise-lasso de-biasing; survival outcomes use the
de-sparsified Cox partial-likelihood estimator.

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  b_inference = "debiased"
)
```

`b_fusion` keeps the coefficient from the chosen fusion model, which is what
drives prediction and the bootstrap selection frequency.

The alternative is a full-pipeline bootstrap: every replicate re-runs the
A-stage, screening and the fused outcome model, so selection uncertainty is
included.

```{r}
fit_boot_b <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  b_inference = "bootstrap",
  bootstrap_repeats = 20,
  sis_n = 25
)
```

With this option `b` is the fusion coefficient and `p_b` is its sign-based
bootstrap p-value (equivalent to inverting the bootstrap percentile interval at
zero; replicates in which the mediator is not selected count as `b* = 0`). The
table also carries `p_b_bootstrap` and the `b_boot_*` interval columns. Use
more replicates (for example 200 or more) in real analyses; the small number
above, and the supplementary early fusion, only keep the example fast.

Mediators removed by screening, or not de-biased, are not B-stage tested
(`tested_b_stage = FALSE`) and receive `p_primary = 1` and `q_primary = 1`, so
FDR is controlled over every feature, not only over the screened subset.

# Stage 5: Combining mediator evidence

For each mediator, Zentangler reports (among other columns):

```text
a                A-path estimate
p_a              A-path p-value
b                B-path estimate (de-biased, or the fusion coefficient)
se_b             standard error of b (de-biased B-path)
p_b              B-path p-value
b_fusion         coefficient from the fusion outcome model
score            a * b
abs_score        abs(score)
tested_b_stage   whether the mediator was tested in the B-stage
p_primary        joint evidence p-value, max(p_a, p_b)
q_primary        final FDR-adjusted value used for discoveries
in_effect_set    whether the mediator entered the causal-effect stage
indirect_effect  mediator-specific indirect effect (effect set only, NA otherwise)
prop_nie         share of the total indirect effect carried by the mediator
```

The main ranking score is `score = a * b`.

Mediation requires both paths, so the null hypothesis for each mediator is the
composite `a = 0 or b = 0`. `p_primary = max(p_a, p_b)` is the joint
significance p-value. How q-values are computed from it is controlled by
`fdr_joint`:

- `fdr_joint = "hdmt"` (default) uses a composite-null FDR estimator in the
  spirit of HDMT (Dai, Stanford and LeBlanc, 2020). Because many features have
  `a = 0` or `b = 0` but not both, applying BH to `max(p_a, p_b)` is very
  conservative; the HDMT-style step estimates the share of each kind of null
  and is less conservative while still controlling FDR.
- `fdr_joint = "maxp"` applies `fdr_method` (BH or BY) directly to
  `p_primary`. This is the simple, conservative alternative.

```{r}
fit_maxp <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fdr_joint = "maxp",
  sis_n = 25
)
summary(fit_maxp)$model
```

These q-values are used for screening and ranking under the selected model.
They should not be described as final post-selection-valid causal inference.

# Multiple-testing scope

Zentangler separates two choices that are easy to confuse:

1. Which FDR correction method should be used?
2. What family of hypotheses should the final q-values be adjusted over?

The correction method is controlled by `fdr_method` (used directly by
`fdr_joint = "maxp"` and by bootstrap-score p-values):

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fdr_method = "BH"
)
```

`fdr_method = "BH"` uses Benjamini-Hochberg. This is the usual default.
`fdr_method = "BY"` uses Benjamini-Yekutieli, which is more conservative and can
be useful when dependence across tests is a major concern.

The final q-value family is controlled by `fdr_scope`:

```{r}
fit_global <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fdr_scope = "global"
)

fit_within <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fdr_scope = "within_view"
)
```

`fdr_scope = "global"` adjusts the final primary p-values across all mediators
from all assay views. This treats the full multiview mediator search as one
multiple-testing family.

`fdr_scope = "within_view"` adjusts the final primary p-values separately inside
each assay view. This treats each view as its own multiple-testing family.

The mediator table keeps both q-value columns regardless of which scope is
selected:

```text
q_primary_global       final q-value adjusted across all views
q_primary_within_view  final q-value adjusted separately within each view
q_primary              q-value used by the current fit, based on fdr_scope
```

This makes it possible to compare global and within-view calls after fitting,
without changing the A-stage or B-stage model.

# Optional bootstrap uncertainty

Besides `b_inference = "bootstrap"`, two further options use bootstrap
resampling:

- `primary_inference = "bootstrap_score"` re-runs the whole pipeline in every
  replicate and uses the sign-based bootstrap p-value of `score = a * b`
  (`p_score_boot`) as `p_primary`. The table also gains `score_boot_*` interval
  columns and `score_boot_selection_freq`.
- `causal_inference = "bootstrap"` adds bootstrap intervals to the causal
  effects for the fixed set of significant mediators (columns such as
  `nie_total_boot_low` / `nie_total_boot_high`).

```{r}
fit_boot <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  primary_inference = "bootstrap_score",
  causal_inference = "bootstrap",
  bootstrap_repeats = 20,
  bootstrap_ci_level = 0.95,
  sis_n = 25,
  seed = 1
)
zentangler_effects(fit_boot)
```

For repeated-measure or longitudinal data, use `bootstrap_id` to resample at the
subject level rather than treating repeated observations as independent samples.

```{r}
fit_boot_subject <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  causal_inference = "bootstrap",
  bootstrap_repeats = 20,
  bootstrap_id = "subject_id",
  sis_n = 25
)
```

Subject-level bootstrap is usually more appropriate when multiple samples come
from the same subject.

# Inspecting outputs

The main results live in three fields of the fit: `fit$mediators` (one row per
feature), `fit$effects` (one-row causal effect summary) and `fit$diagnostics`.
The accessors below return them in a convenient form. Here we use the main fit
from the beginning of the vignette.

```{r}
fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  covariates = "age",
  sis_n = 25
)
```

The full mediator table is available as:

```{r}
all_mediators <- zentangler_mediators(fit)
head(all_mediators)
```

The top-ranked mediators (by `abs_score` unless `order_by` is given) are
available with:

```{r}
zentangler_mediators(fit, top = 20)
zentangler_mediators(fit, top = 10, order_by = "q_primary")
```

Active mediators can be extracted by q-value threshold:

```{r}
zentangler_mediators(fit, q_threshold = 0.25)
```

`summary()` collects a model-level summary, per-view counts, threshold counts,
the top and active mediators, the causal effects and a short interpretation:

```{r}
fit_summary <- summary(fit, q_threshold = 0.25)
names(fit_summary)
fit_summary$model
fit_summary$views
fit_summary
```

The summary can also evaluate several q-value thresholds from the same fitted
model:

```{r}
fit_summary <- summary(
  fit,
  q_threshold = seq(0.05, 0.25, by = 0.05)
)

fit_summary$thresholds
```

This does not refit the model. It only re-counts active mediators under each
threshold (the largest threshold is used for `views` and `active`).

The fit object also contains a `diagnostics` field:

```{r}
fit$diagnostics
```

This includes sample counts, feature counts before and after filtering,
screened mediator counts, non-zero fusion coefficients per view, the number of
B-stage tested mediators, runtime, and bootstrap failures if any occurred.

# Effect decomposition

The fit object includes a one-row causal effect table:

```{r}
zentangler_effects(fit)
```

Mediators with `q_primary <= effect_q_threshold` (default `0.25`) and a non-zero
`b` form the effect set (`in_effect_set` in the mediator table). For this set,
Zentangler reports natural-direct-effect (`nde`), natural-indirect-effect
(`nie_total`), total-effect (`te`) and proportion-mediated summaries by
parametric g-computation. For binary exposures, the default contrast is the
lower observed exposure level versus the higher observed exposure level. For
continuous exposures, the default contrast is the 25th versus 75th percentile,
unless `effect_x0` and `effect_x1` are supplied by the user.

```{r}
fit_strict <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae = mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  covariates = "age",
  sis_n = 25,
  effect_q_threshold = 0.05
)
zentangler_effects(fit_strict)
summary(fit_strict)$interpretation
```

The same table also includes `reduced_total_effect`, which is the reduced
`X -> Y` total-effect estimate, and `p_reduced_total_effect`, which reports the
model-based significance of that reduced total-effect fit.

For Gaussian outcomes, effects are reported on the mean-difference scale. For
binary outcomes, effects are reported on the risk-difference scale by averaging
predicted probabilities under the relevant counterfactual mediator values. For
survival outcomes, effects are reported on the log-hazard-ratio scale.

Mediator-level indirect effects are in the mediator table:

```{r}
zentangler_mediators(fit, q_threshold = 0.25)[
  , c("omics", "mediator", "indirect_effect", "prop_nie", "in_effect_set")
]
```

# Checking recovery on simulated data

Because the example data were simulated, we know the true mediators (`truth`).
A short helper counts true and false positives among the active mediators:

```{r}
score_recovery <- function(fit, truth, q = 0.25) {
  active <- zentangler_mediators(fit, q_threshold = q)
  found <- paste(active$omics, active$mediator, sep = "::")
  data.frame(
    q_threshold = q,
    n_active = length(found),
    true_active = sum(found %in% truth),
    false_active = sum(!(found %in% truth)),
    recall = mean(truth %in% found),
    fdr = if (length(found) > 0) mean(!(found %in% truth)) else 0
  )
}

do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25), score_recovery, fit = fit, truth = truth))
```

Binary outcomes fit the Y-stage with `y_family = "binomial"`:

```{r}
binary_fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y_binary",
  y_family = "binomial",
  covariates = "age",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  b_inference = "debiased",
  sis_n = 25,
  screen_method = "sis",
  seed = 1
)

head(zentangler_mediators(binary_fit))
score_recovery(binary_fit, truth)
```

Survival outcomes are stored as `time` plus 0/1 `status`. For quick checks
without bootstrap, use the survival-aware de-biased B-stage:

```{r}
surv_fit <- fit_multiview_parallel_zentangler(
  mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_family = "survival",
  survival_time_var = "time",
  survival_event_var = "status",
  covariates = "age",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  b_inference = "debiased",
  sis_n = 25,
  screen_method = "sis",
  seed = 1
)

head(zentangler_mediators(surv_fit))
score_recovery(surv_fit, truth)
```

Larger simulation benchmarks (many replicates, several simulation designs and
comparisons with other methods) are not part of the package; the benchmarking
scripts are maintained separately.

# Sequential model

When the views have a natural order (for example taxa -> metabolites), the
sequential model chains mediators along a route of views,
`X -> M1 -> M2 -> Y`. It uses the same entry point with
`model = "sequential"` and a `route`:

```{r}
seq_fit <- zentangler(
  mae,
  model = "sequential",
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  route = c("view1", "view2"),
  covariates = "age",
  sis_n = 25
)
seq_fit
zentangler_paths(seq_fit, q_threshold = 0.25)
```

The views in this simulation are independent given `X`, so few or no
sequential paths are expected here. When `route` is given, `model` can be
omitted. The sequential vignette shows a full analysis.

# Negative controls and direction checks

Two helpers calibrate discoveries. `run_negative_controls()` permutes the
outcome (keeping `X`, covariates and mediators fixed), refits the model for
every permutation and reports permutation p-values for the number of
discoveries, the best q-value and the largest score. Use a few hundred
permutations in practice.

```{r}
nc <- run_negative_controls(
  mae,
  x_var = "X",
  y_var = "Y",
  n_perm = 5,
  q_threshold = 0.25,
  covariates = "age",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  sis_n = 25
)
nc$observed_summary
nc$empirical_summary
head(nc$empirical_units)
```

`run_direction_check()` refits the model with exposure and outcome swapped and
compares the evidence in both directions. It is a directional sensitivity
analysis, not a causal proof.

```{r}
dc <- run_direction_check(
  mae,
  forward_x = "X",
  forward_y = "Y",
  q_threshold = 0.25,
  covariates = "age",
  fusion = "integrated_learner",
  integrated_learner_fusion = "early",
  sis_n = 25
)
dc$summary
dc$comparison
```
